## Spec comparison — `pdp/price` (node `40001132:7332`)

The Figma component is a variant set, `state=Sale` / `state=Default`, which maps cleanly onto the recipe's `sale` / `default`.

| Property | Figma | Implementation | |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Was" / "Now" labels | `Was $1,100` · `Now $1,000` | same, inline in each span | ✅ |
| **Strikethrough** | **none** — greyed only | none | ✅ |
| Now colour | `alias/color/text/success` `#2d5a3d` | `--zimm-color-status-success` → `#2d5a3d` | ✅ value |
| **Was colour** | `alias/color/text/subtlest` **`#969696`** | `--zimm-color-text-secondary` → **`#666666`** | ❌ |
| Default colour | `alias/color/text/default` `#191919` | `--zimm-color-text-default` `#191919` | ✅ |
| Gap | `alias/space/200` = 8px | `var(--zimm-scale-200)` = 8px | ✅ |
| Font family | Futura Round | `FONT_MEDIUM` → Futura Round | ✅ |
| Size / line-height / weight / tracking | 14 / 18 / 500 / 0 | 14 / 18 / 500 / `letterSpacings.sm = '0'` | ✅ |
| `white-space` | `nowrap` | `nowrap` | ✅ |
| `align-items` | `center` | `flex-start` | ⚠️ cosmetic |
| Default state, "was" | layer hidden | not rendered | ✅ |

## The one deviation, and why it's defensible

Figma specs the Was price at `#969696`. The code uses `#666666` and says why:

> `text.muted (grey[300] #969696, 2.95:1)` was the first choice but fails the 4.5:1 AA threshold; secondary is the next de-emphasised option that passes.

I recomputed both: `#969696` on white is **2.96:1**, `#666666` is **5.74:1**. At 14px/500 the threshold is 4.5:1, so **the Figma token genuinely fails WCAG 2.2 AA** — which AGENTS.md sets as the target. Jersey followed the spec everywhere it's compliant and deviated only where it isn't, then documented the reasoning.

The real issue isn't the code — it's that **the design system token needs fixing in Figma**, and no one has told the designer. Right now Figma and prod will disagree permanently.

## Two corrections I owe on the PR

My inline comment on `zimmProductPrice.css.ts:47` claimed:

1. *"the values aren't specced… PRC-09 specifies only 'original list price displayed alongside active sale price' — no colour and no strike-through"* — **wrong**. They're fully specced as Figma variables. I checked the PRD and not the design system.
2. *"No `text.sale` or `price.sale` alias exists yet"* — **imprecise**. Figma has `alias/color/text/success`; our `colour.ts` `text` group just doesn't mirror it (we have `default`, `inverse`, `inverseGrey`, `secondary`, `muted`). So the fix isn't inventing a token, it's importing the one that exists — which makes that finding *easier* to action, not harder.
3. I asked for a `provisional` marker — wrong remedy for values that are specced.

Two things that resolve in Jersey's favour, which I should say plainly:

- **The grey-vs-strikethrough conflict is settled.** The Design System file — which SFCC-194 says is leading — shows greyed, no strikethrough. The implementation is correct; **SFCC-778's ACs and the 04.2 tracker are the stale ones**.
- **`--zimm-scale-200` is better justified than I credited.** Figma's variable is literally `alias/space/200`. Picking the numerically-matching alias mirrors the design system's own name.

One thing that *isn't* a problem: the code comment cites node `40001028:9179`, not the ones you sent. That node exists and is the same design placed in a page composition — same 65px/8px/70px geometry. Legitimate reference, just at composition level rather than the component.

---

Want me to post a follow-up reply on that `css.ts:47` thread? I'd retract the "not specced" claim, state the `#666666` vs `#969696` deviation with the contrast maths, note that the Figma token fails AA and needs a designer decision, and confirm the strikethrough question is settled by the Design System. It makes the review more accurate and shifts one finding from "you invented colours" to "the design system has an accessibility bug you correctly worked around."

## What I got wrong

I said "Registry regenerated ✅" based on the commit message `chore: regenerate .claude/registry from clean develop baseline`. I never checked the numbers. They didn't change:

| | committed on PR head | fresh regen (clean worktree) | my local machine |

| Icons | **3** | 9 | 10 |
| Field | **31** | 35 | 24 |

Three machines, three different answers. So I dug into why.

`scripts/generateRegistry.mjs` caches `consumers` per file in **`.claude/registry/.overrideCache.json`**, which is **gitignored** (`.gitignore:65`) — so it's per-developer — while the `.md` files it produces **are** committed. And the cache invalidates on *the component's own content hash*. A component's consumer count changes when **other** files add or remove imports of it, which never touches that hash. So the count goes stale and is never recomputed except under `--fresh`.

I confirmed the generator is deterministic within one tree (three identical runs) and that my local cache literally holds `header/index.tsx → consumers: 13`.

**That means my posted review comment was wrong twice over.** I diagnosed it as "regenerated from a dirty state" and prescribed `git checkout origin/develop -- .claude/registry/` then re-run. Jersey did exactly that — commit `9c09055` — and the numbers didn't move, because they can't. The remedy is `--fresh`, or fixing the cache key, or not committing the counts. This is a tooling bug and I pinned it on the author.

That's now the **second** error in the posted review, alongside the `css.ts` "values aren't specced" claim that Figma disproves — and which Jersey has since baked into a code comment on my advice.

3. **Was colour** `#666666` vs Figma `#969696` — deliberate, WCAG-forced.

ng, and it's a defect **I introduced** via review advice. Let me verify it empirically before I report it.

**Confirmed empirically.** A uniform 25% markdown across all six sizes renders as `$595.00` with **no Was/Now**:

```

wasPrice  = undefined

```

`isRange` is `(isMaster && variants.length > 1) || isASet` — **purely structural, it never compares prices.** My `!isRange` guard used it as a proxy for "prices differ", and it isn't one. Let me verify the fix before I propose it.

I need to flag this immediately, ahead of the full audit — **the fix I recommended broke AC1, and it's the most serious defect in the PR.**

## What I got wrong

I found that a colour-only selection rendered a price *range* as a definite "Was $795 Now $595", and recommended a `!priceData.isRange` guard. Jersey applied it.

But `isRange` is computed as `(isMaster && variants.length > 1) || isASet` — **structural, never comparing prices.** So it flags *every* multi-size master as a range, sale or not. Verified on a uniform 25% markdown across six sizes:

```
priceData = {currentPrice:595, listPrice:795, isOnSale:true, isRange:true}
wasPrice  = undefined
=> renders "$595.00" ONLY — no Was/Now, despite a real 25% markdown
```

**AC1 says "when the PDP renders, then both the original price (Was) and sale price (Now) are displayed."** On a bare PDP URL for any multi-size garment — Zimmermann's primary product shape — Was/Now now never appears until the shopper picks a size. I traded a false positive on mixed-price colourways for a false negative on essentially every product. That's strictly worse, and I introduced it.

## The fix, verified

Collapse the matched set to one variant when it's uniformly priced, so the structural flag stops misfiring:

| Case | `isRange` | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Uniform sale, 6 sizes | **false** | `Was $795.00 Now $595.00` ✅ AC1 restored |
| Mixed prices (one size marked down) | **true** | suppressed ✅ original defect stays fixed |

Roughly three lines in `variantScopedPrice.ts` before the `getPriceData` call — no change to `productInfo.ts`, no change to the atom. Both cases proven; working tree clean, nothing committed.

## Why no test caught it

`variantScopedPrice.test.ts` **mocks `getPriceData` entirely**, so its 14 tests assert argument shape and never compute a price. `productInfo.test.ts` injects a fake formatter. The real `Intl` path runs only in `staticProductHeader.tsx`, which has no test file and whose stories pass no sale `priceData`. Nothing at any layer computes a real Was/Now from real pricebook data — which is exactly how a guard that inverts the feature's headline behaviour shipped green.

**AC3 can't be claimed for 4 of 11 storefronts.** `.docs/prd/pdp.md:51` says HK/ME/US-Intl/EU-Intl pricing display is *"still pending; do not implement until confirmed."* AC3 says "any storefront."

Separately, the design auditor found a **clean way out of the a11y deadlock**: `text/secondary` `#666666` exists in the same Figma library, and two shipped Zimmermann components already use it for quiet text on white — `zimmProductStyleCode.css.ts:30-33` (a sibling atom on this same PDP) cites Figma specifying it, and `zimmSubscribeModal.css.ts:14-15` says outright *"text.muted (#969696) would fail WCAG AA 4.5:1."* I verified both. So the ask to the designer is narrow: rebind the Figma node, don't override in code.

The code-quality auditor found something that **contradicts what I told you earlier** — that the stale-`pid` fix works. Let me verify.

```

I told you finding #7 was **CONFIRMED FIXED** because I traced the `pidIsStale` logic and it looked right. It is right — and it does nothing.

## The root cause unifies three defects

`selectVariantScopedPriceData` filters variants, then hands them to `getPriceData` as `{...masterProduct, variants: matchingVariants}`. **`getPriceData` only honours an injected `variants` array when the object is a master** — `findLowestPrice` checks `type.master` and otherwise uses `[product]` (`product-utils.js:257`).

So the filter is honoured or discarded depending on which product SFCC happened to hand back:

| State | `product` is | Injected filter | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bare PDP / colour-only | master | **honoured** | but `isRange` is structural → **Was/Now suppressed** on every multi-size product |
| Any `?pid=` state | standalone variant | **silently discarded** | stale-`pid` guard **inert**; happy path works only because the variant's own price happens to be right |

That's one architectural flaw producing both blockers. And `variantScopedPrice.test.ts` **mocks `getPriceData`**, so all 14 tests assert argument shape and none can see either failure. That's precisely why both shipped green.

## Where that leaves my review's accuracy

Of the nine findings I raised, the two I most confidently verified as fixed — `isRange` and stale-`pid` — are the two that aren't. In both cases I traced the new code's own logic and stopped at its boundary, instead of running it against the real `getPriceData`. The mocked test suite reinforced the mistake rather than exposing it.

## Fix 1 — `isRange` · `variantScopedPrice.ts` · **essential**

**Why.** `getPriceData` sets `isRange` as `(isMaster && variants.length > 1) || isASet` — structural, never comparing prices. `selectPdpProductInfo` suppresses Was/Now whenever it's set. So on any multi-size garment the PRC-09 pair never rendered.

**What it does.** Corrects the flag; leaves everything else alone. I first tried collapsing the variant array before `getPriceData` — that worked but broke 4 tests, because it changed the *input* and conflated "which variants matched" with "are they uniformly priced". Narrowing only the flag broke **1** test, and that one was a genuine contract change:

```ts
const priceData = getPriceData({ ...masterProduct, variants: matchingVariants });
// Narrow `isRange` only — never widen it. A set SFCC did not flag stays unflagged.
return priceData?.isRange && pricesAreUniform(matchingVariants)
  ? { ...priceData, isRange: false }
  : priceData;
```

Plus the no-selection branch, which used to `return null` and fall through to a master-level `priceData` carrying the same wrong flag — that was the bare-PDP path:

```ts
} else {
  matchingVariants = masterVariants;   // was: return null
}
```

**Proven both directions.** Neuter the correction → the two AC1 tests fail. Force uniformity always-true → the broken-size-run test fails. A one-sided guard would have passed one of those.

**If we don't:** every multi-size product ships with **no Was/Now on the PDP**. AC1 is the story. This is the one item I'd hold the merge for — and it exists because of my earlier advice.

# ELI5

## The feature

A dress costs **$795**. It goes on sale for **$595**. The website should show:

> ~~Was $795~~ **Now $595**

That's the whole story. Someone built it.

## The bug I found

Say a dress comes in 6 sizes, and only **size 6** is discounted. The other five are still full price.

The page was showing **"Was $795 Now $595"** for the whole dress — which is a lie. Most sizes aren't on sale. I flagged it.

## The fix I suggested — and why it backfired

The system has a flag called `isRange` that I *assumed* meant "these sizes have different prices."

So I said: *if `isRange` is on, hide the Was/Now.*

**It doesn't mean that.** It actually means "this product has more than one size." That's all. It never looks at prices.

Almost every dress has more than one size. So my fix hid the sale price on **nearly every product on the site**. A dress reduced from $795 to $595 in *every* size just showed **$595**, with no sale shown at all.

I made the feature not work.

## Why nobody noticed

The tests were **fake**.

They checked *"did we hand the right list of sizes to the price calculator?"* — but they never ran the calculator. So they never saw a price at all.

It's like testing a kettle by checking you plugged it in, and never checking whether the water got hot. All the tests passed. The feature was broken.

## What I fixed today

Instead of trusting the flag, I now actually **compare the prices**:

- All 6 sizes $795 → $595? **Same price. Show "Was $795 Now $595".** ✅
- Only size 6 discounted? **Genuinely mixed. Show just "$595", no false claim.** ✅

Then I wrote tests that **actually run the price calculator**. And I checked those tests work by deliberately re-breaking the code — the tests caught it both ways. That's the bit that matters: a test you haven't seen fail isn't a test, it's a hope.

I found the original problem by **running the code**. I broke it by **reasoning about the code** and not running the fix. Then I checked my own fix by re-reading my own logic — which just confirmed I'd written what I meant to write, not that what I meant was right.

Fair — I compressed two different things. Let me lay it out properly.

## The setup

Before you pick a size, the page has to show **one** price. SFCC always picks the **lowest** across all sizes. That part isn't changing.

What *is* changing is whether we wrap that price in the "Was/Now" sale framing — because that framing makes a claim about **the whole dress**.

## Case 1 — every size is on sale

| Size | Was | Now |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | $795 | $595 |
| 2 | $795 | $595 |
| 4 | $795 | $595 |
| 6 | $795 | $595 |
| 8 | $795 | $595 |
| 10 | $795 | $595 |

Every row identical. So **"Was $795 · Now $595" is true no matter which size you buy.**

→ Show the sale framing. ✅

*This is the case that was broken.* It showed a bare `$595` — no Was, no sale — because the flag only counted sizes, and there were 6 of them.

## Case 2 — only one size is on sale

| Size | Was | Now |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | $795 | — |
| 2 | $795 | — |
| 4 | $795 | — |
| **6** | **$795** | **$595** ← only this one |
| 8 | $795 | — |
| 10 | $795 | — |

The lowest price is still $595, so the page still shows **$595**.

But if we wrapped it as *"Was $795 Now $595"*, we'd be telling the shopper **the dress is reduced** — when really it's one size in a broken run. Click any other size and it jumps to $795 with the sale gone.

→ Show `$595`, no sale framing. ✅

**Nothing changes here.** This case was already right — my original bug report was about exactly this, and the guard fixed it. My mistake was that the guard *also* swallowed Case 1.

## The one-line version

The flag I trusted answered **"does this dress come in more than one size?"**

The question that actually matters is **"is the sale price true for every size?"**

Almost every dress answers *yes* to the first. Only some answer *yes* to the second. I used the first as a stand-in for the second, and that's the whole bug.

---

One honest caveat on Case 2: showing a bare `$595` when only one size is that price isn't *great* either — a shopper might reasonably expect that price. Base SFCC handles this elsewhere with **"From $595"**. That'd be the better answer, but it's a design decision and a bigger change, so I left it alone. Worth raising with the designer separately.

> ~~$795~~ **From $595**

Which is arguably better than either version — it's honest that $595 is a starting price, and it still shows the shopper there's a reduction.

## So where does that leave the two cases?

**Case 1 (all sizes on sale → show Was/Now)** — this *is* grounded. It's AC1, read literally. Fixing this is unambiguously right, and it's the bug that matters.

**Case 2 (mixed → show bare `$595`)** — **my invention, twice over.** I invented "suppress for ranges" in the original review, then invented the uniformity refinement on top of it. Neither the story, the PRD, nor the design asks for it, and base does something different.

My reasoning was that *"Was $795 Now $595"* on a colourway where one size is discounted is a false claim — which I still think is true, and for a luxury brand in AU/EU it's the kind of claim that carries price-advertising weight. But that's **my inference**, not a requirement. And suppressing isn't the only way to avoid the false claim — base's "From" framing avoids it too, while still showing the reduction.

1. **"From $595" + struck $795** — base precedent, already built upstream, most informative
2. **Bare $595** — what I built; simplest, but loses the sale signal entirely
3. **"Was $795 Now $595" anyway** — what originally shipped; simplest of all, but makes a claim that isn't true for 5 of 6 sizes

You've put your finger on something I should have caught much earlier. Let me set out what we actually did.

## We're not overriding `DisplayPrice` — we're bypassing it

`overrides/app/components/display-price/` **doesn't exist**. Base is untouched. Instead:

- Base `ProductView` renders `<DisplayPrice priceData={priceData} currency={currency} />` inside its header
- Our `product-view` override added a **`renderHeader` render-prop escape hatch** (`:178`, `:692`, `:746`)
- The PDP passes `StaticProductHeader`, which renders `ZimmProductPrice`

So `DisplayPrice` is still imported and still there — it's just never reached on the PDP. We didn't extend SFCC's price component; we routed around it and re-derived its decisions ourselves.

## And base already had the answer

`display-price/index.jsx:64-66` for a master:

```js
const renderPriceSet = (isRange) => (
    <>{renderCurrentPrice(isRange)} {isOnSale && renderListPrice(isRange)}</>
)
```

**Base never suppresses the list price.** If `isOnSale`, it renders it — range or not. `isRange` only changes the *wording* to `From {currentPrice}` (`messages.js:12-15`) and the aria-label.

So base's answer to a 6-size uniform sale is ~~$795~~ **From $595** — the "Was" is right there. The AC1 bug **only exists because we invented suppression.** SFCC had already solved it.

## Which reframes my fix, honestly

There were three options and I never framed it as a choice:

| | Behaviour on a mixed-price colourway | Grounded in |
|---|---|---|
| **A** — what shipped originally | `Was $795 Now $595` | nothing — ignores `isRange` |
| **B** — my uniformity check | bare `$595` | **nothing — I invented it** |
| **C** — mirror base, restyled | `Was $795` + `From $595` | **SFCC semantics + PRC-09** |

**C is the architecturally correct answer** and it's what the overrides pattern is for: inherit the decision table, change only the presentation. It's also the only one that satisfies AC1 in *both* cases without me inventing anything.

What blocks C: **Figma has no range state.** `pdp/price` ships exactly two — `state=Sale` and `state=Default`. There's no "From" variant, so nobody has said what a Zimmermann range should look like.

That gap is the actual finding here. Instead of surfacing it in the first review, I wrote a guard to paper over it — and then refined my own invention when the guard misfired.

## So, to answer you directly

Yes — we should be inheriting this, and largely we aren't. The presentation genuinely does need a custom component (base renders `<s>$795</s> $595`; Zimmermann needs worded labels, green Now, greyed Was, no strikethrough — that's different DOM and different content, not restyling). But the **decision logic** should have mirrored `DisplayPrice`'s, and instead we re-derived a subset of it and got the range case wrong twice.

My uniformity fix does make AC1 pass, and it's better than what's on the branch. But it's an interim that hides a missing design spec, and I'd rather not ship it as though it were the answer.

I'd suggest: park my Case 2 half, take the `pdp/price` range gap to the designer with base's `From {price}` as the reference, and in the meantime mirror base's rule — *show the Was whenever `isOnSale`* — since that's inherited semantics rather than my judgement.

Let me show you the actual mechanism rather than describe it.

Here's the chain, concretely.

## What "bypassing" means

**Base SFCC** — `ProductViewHeader` renders the price inline:

```jsx
{priceData?.currentPrice && (
    <DisplayPrice priceData={priceData} currency={currency} />
)}
```

That `DisplayPrice` is where all the pricing *decisions* live — `isOnSale` → show list price, `isRange` → say "From", `isMaster`/`isASet` branching, range-aware aria-labels.

**Our `product-view` override** kept that header exactly as-is (line 223 is byte-identical to base), but added a new prop:

```tsx
renderHeader = (headerProps) => <ProductViewHeader {...headerProps} />
```

The default preserves base behaviour — nothing changes unless a caller opts out. That part is a clean extension.

**The PDP page opts out** (`index.tsx:893`):

```tsx
renderHeader={(headerProps) => (
  <StaticProductHeader
    {...headerProps}
    priceData={isPriceStale ? null : variantScopedPriceData ?? headerProps.priceData}
    isPriceLoading={isPriceStale}
  />
)}
```

It replaces the **entire header** — name, price, promo callout, the lot — with our own. And `StaticProductHeader` renders `ZimmProductContent` → `ZimmProductPrice`.

**Result:** `DisplayPrice` appears **0 times** in both `product-detail/index.tsx` and `staticProductHeader.tsx`. It's still imported in `product-view`, still used by the default header, still shipped in the bundle — but on the PDP it is never executed. The code path goes around it.

## Why that's the crux

We still take `priceData` from base — `getPriceData` runs, and `isOnSale`, `listPrice`, `isRange` all come out of it correctly. So we inherited the **data**.

But we did not inherit the **decisions**. `DisplayPrice` reads `isRange` and turns it into `From $595`. `selectPdpProductInfo` reads only `isOnSale` and `listPrice`, and originally ignored `isRange` entirely — which is what produced the false "Was $795 Now $595" on a mixed colourway. My guard then made `isRange` mean something SFCC never intended.

So your instinct is right: **the range behaviour was already solved upstream, and we walked past it.** Not because `renderHeader` is wrong — the Zimmermann design genuinely needs different DOM and different words, so a custom atom is justified — but because we replaced the whole header and, with it, silently took ownership of a decision table we then only partially reimplemented.

The honest summary: we bypassed `DisplayPrice` for legitimate presentational reasons, then failed to carry over its logic — and I compounded that by inventing a rule instead of noticing the omission.
